SOURCE: "Tutorial Proposal: Retrieval-based Language Models and Applications", Akari Asai, Sewon Min, Zexuan Zhong, Danqi Chen (UW / Princeton). Proceedings of ACL 2023, Vol. 6: Tutorial Abstracts, pp. 41–46, July 9, 2023.

COVERAGE: I read all 24,657 of 24,657 chars, which is all 6 pages. That covers the description, outline, tutorial information, presenter bios, reading list and references. I skimmed the bios and references for origins only. The figure-caption script returned nothing, so the document has no figures.

The document is a tutorial proposal. It runs no experiments, reports no results, has no tables and gives no numbers about model behaviour. Its only numbers are logistics: 3 hours, an audience of 150+, and 20%/80% presenters' own work vs others'. Beyond the taxonomies below there is little to cite, and every benefit it claims is someone else's result, cited without figures.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: It sorts retrieval-based LMs by how the retrieved information enters the model, in three classes. Input: retrieved text is concatenated with the input (Lewis 2020, i.e. RAG; Guu 2020, i.e. REALM; Izacard 2022b, i.e. Atlas). Intermediate layers: retrieval is latent and fused inside the Transformer (de Jong 2022; Févry 2020; Borgeaud 2022, i.e. RETRO). Output: the LM's token distribution is interpolated with one built from what was retrieved (Khandelwal 2020, i.e. kNN-LM; Zhong 2022; Yogatama 2021, i.e. SPALM).

  setup: taxonomy only, no evaluation

WHEN TO RETRIEVE: the tutorial has no "when to retrieve" dimension. Its taxonomies cover what is retrieved (granularity) and how it is used (input, intermediate or output layer). The only related remark is open question (2), quoted under LIMITS, and it asks when retrieval-based LMs are useful at all, not when to retrieve during generation. Do not attribute a "when" axis to this source.

LIMITS:
- The authors list three open problems: "(1) how we can further improve the scalability of retrieval-based LMs without sacrificing performance, (2) when retrieval-based LMs are particularly useful in the era of rapidly evolving LMs, and (3) what is necessary to enable applications of retrieval-based LMs for more diverse domains." (p.42)
- They concede that training is hard because the datastore is large: "how to train retrieval-based LMs effectively and efficiently remains challenging." (p.41)
- Ethics section (p.43): retrieval-based LMs "can still be plausible sounding but incorrect or non-sensical outputs". Because they "may retrieve raw data from a corpus, which can leak privacy-sensitive information, especially when they are built on top of a private corpus". It says prior work "shows" retrieval reduces bias and hallucination but gives no citation at that point.
- It is dated: the proposal was written before ICL-era RAG with API models became dominant. It treats prompting only briefly, and its "LMs" are mostly pre-2023 research models.

BUILDS ON: Lewis et al., 2020 (RAG); Guu et al., 2020 (REALM); Khandelwal et al., 2020 (kNN-LM); Borgeaud et al., 2022 (RETRO); Izacard et al., 2022b (Atlas); Izacard et al., 2022a (Contriever); Zhong et al., 2022 (memory augmentation); Min et al., 2022 (NPM); Févry et al., 2020 (Entities as Experts); de Jong et al., 2022 (Mention Memory); Yogatama et al., 2021 (SPALM); He et al., 2021 and Alon et al., 2022 (datastore and search efficiency); Karpukhin et al., 2020 (DPR); Shi et al., 2022 (kNN-Prompt). It sets itself apart from earlier tutorials: Chen and Yih, 2020 (ACL open-domain QA) and Cai et al., 2022 (SIGIR retrieval-augmented text generation).

CODE: none.

FIGURES: none.

PROBLEMS: The text extracted cleanly. It has only hyphenation line breaks and source typos ("long-rail", "Demostration", "Adaption"). It contains no embedded instructions.

FIT WITH THE NOTES
- Best fit: generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/notes/01-rag-pipeline.md, section "Architectures" > "Naive, advanced, modular", the paragraph after the Gao figure, line 48. That paragraph gives Zhao et al.'s axis of where the retrieved object enters the generator (query-based, latent-representation, logit-based, speculative). Asai et al.'s input / intermediate / output layers match Zhao's first three classes; they have no speculative class.
  - It supports the note: both put RETRO's fusion in the latent/intermediate class and kNN-LM in the logit/output class. The tutorial also predates Zhao by a year.
  - It does not contradict the note anywhere.
  - Its one distinct addition is the granularity axis (token, entity mention or text chunk), which the note does not mention.
  - This is a "sharpens" case: add a citation that this axis predates Zhao, and add a references row. A citation would read "Asai et al., ACL 2023 tutorial, doi 10.18653/v1/2023.acl-tutorials.6", and should say it is a taxonomy with no experiments.
- Secondary fit: generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/notes/02-why-rag-and-the-augmented-prompt.md, section "The two components".
  - The training table (lines 83–89, sequential / joint) matches the tutorial's split of pipelined, fixed-retriever and joint training. Its joint training is either in-batch approximation or asynchronous index refresh, and the note's REALM paragraph (line 93) describes the asynchronous refresh.
  - The note's kNN-LM paragraph (line 95, "act on the model's output") and RETRO paragraph (line 97) match the tutorial's output-layer and intermediate-layer classes.
  - One thing to check: the tutorial puts REALM and Atlas in the input-concatenation class, alongside RAG, even though they are jointly trained. Note 02 does not say otherwise, but if the caller adds an "integration point" label to that section, REALM and Atlas belong under input, not latent. The note's line 99 calls Atlas "a T5 Fusion-in-Decoder reader". Zhao's survey and note 01 line 48 file FiD under latent fusion, so the two taxonomies disagree on where FiD-style readers go. A citation should mention this disagreement rather than ignore it.
- Nothing citable beyond the taxonomies (integration point, granularity, training) and the list of open problems. Every benefit it asserts is second-hand, without numbers. Cite the primary papers for those, as the notes already do.
